articles.title: My search box scored 1.00 on a query it understood nothing about
articles.author: Jianzhujisuan
articles.description:
On 21 November someone typed 18米高8米宽 into the search box on my site. That means "18 m high, 8 m wide" — a question about scaffolding, arriving from a comment thread about a job site. The search returned a table of rebar hook lengths and a chart of bricks per cubic metre of masonry.

Both results were served at a relevance score of 1.00.

The query contains no noun. Not one. It is two dimensions and nothing else, and my matcher looked at it and said: perfect match, here you go.

This is about the arithmetic that made that inevitable, why the obvious fixes don't help, and the four-line gate that replaced a scoring problem with a refusal to guess.

The failure has two stages, and the first one behaved correctly

Search on the site is a plain substring AND over an index string per card. Each card carries a data-k attribute — title, category, a one-line description, the slug, and a handful of pinyin and synonym aliases. Stage one requires every whitespace-separated token of the query to appear somewhere in that string.

// stage 1
n = apply(function (key) {
  for (var i = 0; i < toks.length; i++) {
    if (key.indexOf(toks[i]) < 0) return false;
  }
  return true;
});

Chinese has no spaces, so 18米高8米宽 is one token, and no index string contains it. Zero results. That is correct for stage one, and it is why stage two exists: people type questions, the index stores nouns, and substring matching won't bridge that on its own.

Stage two is a 2-gram fallback. Split the query into CJK bigrams and alphanumeric runs, drop segments that appear nowhere in the index, then score every card:

var gs = raw.match(/[a-z0-9]+|[\u4e00-\u9fff]+/g);   // segment the query
// CJK segment → all overlapping 2-grams; ASCII/digits → kept whole
score = hits / valid.length;                          // fraction of grams found
if (max >= 0.5) showEverythingTiedAtMax();

That "drop segments that appear nowhere" step is the clever part, and it is normally what makes this kind of fallback work at all. A user types 一米多重怎么算; 怎么算 exists on no card, so counting it in the denominator would cap every real match at 20%. Filtering noise out of the denominator is what lets the signal win.

On this query, the filter did its job perfectly — and that is the problem. 米高 and 米宽 are not in the index. Neither is anything else. What survived was the digits.

The score is hits / tokens, which rewards queries it understands least

Two grams survived, so the denominator was 2, so one hit scored 0.5 and cleared the threshold. Required matches is always ceil(n/2): four grams need two, two grams need one, and a single-gram query needs a hit to score a flat 1.00.

Read that back: the less of the query the parser could keep, the lower the bar to answer it. Confidence and comprehension move in opposite directions — the exact inversion of what a relevance score should mean.

The index has 238 cards and 4,204 distinct CJK bigrams, and the frequency distribution is brutally top-heavy:

Bigram Cards containing it Share of index
算器 206 86.6%
计算 187 78.6%
用量 64 26.9%
面积 61 25.6%

Every card title ends in "calculator", so any fragment of that word is universal. A two-gram query where one gram is 计算 scores 0.5 everywhere before it has found out what the page is about.

What the two grams actually were

Here is the part I did not expect. The surviving grams were 18 and 8, and two cards contain both. Both contain them because both index strings contain the number 180:

  • the rebar hook page, whose index text includes 180度弯钩 — a 180-degree hook;
  • the brick table, whose index text includes 120 / 180 / 240 — wall thicknesses in millimetres.

18 and 8 are substrings of 180. One page means degrees, the other means millimetres, and the scoring function saw identical evidence in both. The 1.00 was not a measurement of relevance. It was a coincidence of string layout, and it happened to land on exactly the two cards whose numbers differ in unit from the question that was asked.

Digit fragments are rare in the index, which made the coincidence look like a signal:

Fragment Cards containing it Share
18 2 1%
8 5 2%
1 13 5%
5 14 6%

And because the fallback shows everything tied at the maximum in build order rather than by score, the answer was stable, reproducible, and arbitrary. 1.5米 produced seven cards at 1.00 for the same reason: grams 1 and 5, one hit each, seven winners.

Rarity doesn't rescue you

The reflex fix is IDF — weight rare grams up, common grams down. It makes this worse. 18 appears on 2 of 238 cards, so it is maximally rare, so IDF would push its weight to the ceiling and make the wrong answer more confident.

The confusion is between a rare term and a rare substring. 18 is rare because numbers are fragments of larger numbers, not because it carries meaning. A tokenizer that treats digits as units of evidence is measuring typography, not language. Same reason 8 and 800 and 1800 all look like unrelated, highly specific facts.

The gate: does the query still contain a subject?

I stopped trying to make the score smarter and put a check in front of it instead. Strip the units, the dimension words, the numerals and the question particles. If nothing is left, the query is not a document lookup — it is a parameter lookup, and a search box has no business answering it.

var MEASURE = /米|厘米|毫米|公分|吨|公斤|千克|kg|mm|cm|多高|多宽|多长|多重|多厚|多少|几个|几根|几块|几米|[0-9.\s]/g;

function hasSignal(raw) {
  var t = raw.replace(MEASURE, "").replace(/高|宽|长|厚|重|大|小|的/g, "");
  // a CJK noun survived, or an identifier like hrb400 / c30 / pavement
  return /[\u4e00-\u9fff]/.test(t) || /[a-z]{2,}/.test(t);
}

Two details matter. The strip list is deliberately greedy — 高宽长厚重 are the words people use to describe a dimension, and leaving them in would let 18米高 pass as a subject. The second clause keeps real identifiers alive: hrb400 and c30 are not measurements, and killing them would break every steel and concrete query on the site.

When the gate returns false, the fallback does not run, and the UI says nothing was found and offers the category list. Zero results beats a plausible wrong one, because the two failures have different costs. Someone who gets nothing retypes the query. Someone who gets a hook-length table concludes the site doesn't have a scaffolding calculator and leaves.

Measured, before and after

Twenty dimension-only queries — 18米高8米宽, 6米跨度, 4.5米层高, 300高, 0.5米厚, and so on — run against the same 238-card index, with the old fallback and the gated one:

Answered Relevant
Old fallback 19 / 20 0 / 19
Gated 3 / 20 0 / 3

Nineteen out of twenty got an answer, and not one of them was about the right thing. That is the shape of the bug: not a rare wrong answer, but a system that answered almost everything and was almost never right.

I'll be straight about the residual. Three still get through, because 跨度 and 层高 are genuine nouns even though the query is a dimension: 6米跨度 returns four cards, 4.5米层高 returns two (paint coverage and wallpaper, both of which mention ceiling height in passing). And 18米高8米宽间距1.5 returns fourteen, because 间距 survives the strip — it is a real word, and it is also the one word in that sentence that describes a parameter rather than a product. A vocabulary of parameter nouns would fix those. I haven't built it, and I'd rather ship the gate that removes 16 wrong answers than wait for the one that removes 19.

The second-order cost, in the analytics

Every search reports its result count. Zero-result queries are the useful ones: a demand list of things people asked for that the site doesn't have, which I read every morning.

For as long as the fallback answered these queries, they never appeared as misses. The 18 × 8 m scaffold, the 6 m span, the wall thickness — all recorded as successful searches. The bug didn't just serve the wrong page; it deleted the evidence that the page was missing. Two weeks of demand data, silently scored 1.00.

That is the part I'd flag to anyone with a hand-rolled matcher: a false positive in search is also a false negative in your product backlog, and only one of those is visible to the user.

Reproducing it

The harness reads the built index.html, pulls every card's data-k, and runs both versions of the fallback against the same 20 queries:

score = sum(1 for g in valid if g in key) / len(valid)   # identical to the JS
if max_score >= 0.5: winners = [c for c in cards if s(c) >= max_score - 1e-9]

Run it against your own index and look at two numbers: how many cards tie at the maximum, and how many of the query's surviving grams are digits or fragments of digits. If both are non-zero, your fallback is answering questions it cannot read.

The site this came from is jianzhujisuan.com, a set of construction-quantity calculators with 238 tools on the index. The scaffolding page is the one that visitor was actually looking for, and it took a comment-section bug report for the search box to stop hiding it.

The lesson I keep re-learning, in one line: a relevance score is a claim about the query, not about the page. Mine was computed entirely from the page, and so it was 1.00 on a query that had nothing in it to be relevant to.

articles.title: Shopify script tag deprecation: find what stops working on March 1, 2027
articles.author: Hamza Ahmad Aslam
articles.description:
Originally published at hamzaahmadaslam.com.

How this article was made: drafted with AI assistance from a researched brief, then checked against primary documentation before publishing.

Shopify script tag deprecation means apps that still load storefront code through the old ScriptTag API will stop doing so on March 1, 2027. You can find the affected scripts in your storefront's page source, match them to installed apps and check whether each replacement is active before the deadline.

What changes on March 1, 2027?

Shopify will stop injecting script tags into storefront pages on March 1, 2027. If your reviews, chat, pop-ups or another feature still depends on one, that feature will stop loading. Your Shopify admin will not necessarily show an error.

A script tag lets an app load JavaScript without editing theme code. Shopify introduced theme app extensions as the replacement in 2021.

Shopify's changelog post of August 24, 2026 and its developer guides establish these dates:

Date What changes
August 28, 2025 Script tags stop running on the Order status page for Shopify Plus stores.
August 26, 2026 Script tags stop running on the Order status page for all other stores.
October 1, 2026 Apps can no longer create or update script tags on any Admin API version. Existing tags keep running.
March 1, 2027 Shopify stops injecting script tags into storefronts. Features still depending on them stop loading.

The October restriction affects GraphQL scriptTagCreate and scriptTagUpdate, plus REST POST and PUT. Older API versions cannot bypass it.

The scriptTags query and scriptTagDelete mutation remain available for audits and cleanup.

The storefront deadline also applies to vintage themes. App embed replacements support vintage and Online Store 2.0 themes.

How common are old Shopify script tags?

On November 1, 2026 I checked the public home pages of 206 Shopify storefronts, one request each, reading the script tag list Shopify prints in each page; 120 of them still loaded at least one script tag. It is one day's sample, so read it as a sign of how common this still is, not as a measurement of all stores.

A script tag's presence does not prove that its feature will break. The app might already have a working replacement while its old tag remains installed.

How do you find script tags on your Shopify store?

You can check a public storefront using a desktop browser. You do not need an API token or access to theme code.

Step 1: Open your live storefront

Open your store's public home page in a desktop browser.

Use a logged-out session so you see what customers see. A password-protected store shows its password page instead. Use an authorized session to inspect the actual storefront.

Check the published theme rather than an unpublished preview.

Step 2: View the page source

Right-click the page and choose View page source.

You can also use:

  • Windows or Linux: Ctrl+U
  • macOS Chrome: Cmd+Option+U

The browser opens a tab containing the HTML returned by the server. Use this instead of the Elements panel in developer tools.

Step 3: Search for asyncLoad

Use your browser's Find command and search for:

asyncLoad

Look for a block containing:

var urls = [

Read the web addresses inside the list. Each represents a script tag Shopify is injecting into that page.

The domain often identifies the vendor. The ?shop= parameter commonly contains your store's .myshopify.com address.

Some addresses contain \/ instead of /, or \u0026 instead of &. These are escaped characters in the page source. They do not change the domain.

If there is no asyncLoad block, this check finds no injected script tags on that page. Other JavaScript can still run through theme code or app extensions.

Step 4: Separate old script tags from app embeds

Only the addresses inside the var urls list are the script tags identified by this inspection method.

Script files elsewhere in the page load through other methods and are not affected by this change. App embed files, for example, commonly use cdn.shopify.com addresses containing /extensions/.

Shopify documents that theme app extension assets are hosted on its CDN. The /extensions/ address pattern is something you can observe in page source, not a guaranteed URL format from Shopify's documentation.

Step 5: Match each domain to an installed app

In Shopify admin:

  1. Open Settings > Apps.
  2. Review the installed apps.
  3. Compare their names and vendors with your script domains.
  4. Open each likely app's details or Shopify App Store listing.
  5. Contact the app's support team if you cannot identify a domain.

For example, example-reviews.example might belong to a reviews app. That domain is an illustrative placeholder.

A matching domain is a clue, not proof. Some apps host scripts through separate companies.

Shopify scopes script tags to the app that created them. Uninstalling an app automatically removes its tags. Every address still injected through the list therefore belongs to an installed app.

Recently uninstalled apps matter when investigating theme code left behind, rather than active ScriptTag records.

How do you make a script tag inventory?

Copy this table into a document or spreadsheet. Record one row per address.

All rows, domains and app names below are illustrative examples.

Script address (domain) App or vendor Still used? Replacement Done on published theme?
example-reviews.example (illustrative) Example Reviews Yes App embed No
example-chat.example (illustrative) Example Chat Yes App embed Yes
example-tracking.example (illustrative) Example Tracking Unknown Web pixel No

For each row, keep the full URL alongside the domain. A developer may need it to identify the exact record.

Use the final column to record whether the replacement works on the published storefront. Web pixels do not require a theme-editor activation step.

What should replace each script tag?

The replacement depends on what the code does. Shopify explains the available approaches in its storefront migration documentation.

What the script does Replacement Who handles it
Displays reviews, chat, pop-ups, badges or other storefront features App embed block in a theme app extension App developer builds it; merchant activates it
Collects only analytics or conversion events Web pixel App developer implements it
Sends events to a service without a supported app Custom pixel Merchant or developer maintains it
Belongs to an app the store no longer needs Uninstall the app Store owner or manager
Belongs to an admin-created custom app that cannot use extensions Move into theme code or replace the app Developer or service provider

An app embed can also load JavaScript without displaying a visible widget.

How do you activate a Shopify app embed?

App embeds start disabled after installation. An app cannot activate one automatically for the merchant.

To enable a replacement:

  1. Open Online Store in Shopify admin.
  2. Select Edit theme for the published theme.
  3. Select the App embeds icon in the editor sidebar.
  4. Find the replacement app's embed.
  5. Turn its toggle on.
  6. Select Save.
  7. Check the feature on the live storefront.

These steps follow Shopify's theme app embed instructions.

If the embed is missing, ask the vendor whether its app supports the replacement.

App embeds are enabled per theme. Before publishing another theme, open its App embeds panel and activate the required embeds. Market configurations can also have their own app embed settings, so check those where applicable.

What if the script only tracks visitors or purchases?

Use the vendor's web pixel replacement when available. Web pixels collect customer events without requiring activation in the theme editor.

If no suitable app pixel exists, a developer can consider a custom pixel under Settings > Customer events.

Shopify says adding and using custom pixels is unsupported by Shopify. Some pixel code does not work in the pixel sandbox, so the third-party vendor may need to help.

Remove or modify previous tracking code, including code in theme.liquid, to avoid counting events twice. Follow Shopify's custom pixel instructions.

Why should you avoid running both versions?

Before March 1, 2027, the old tag can run alongside its replacement.

If both execute the same functionality, analytics events might be counted twice or a widget might appear twice.

Keep the old feature working until its replacement is ready. Then have the responsible app remove its old tag.

After the deadline, leftover script tag records no longer load storefront code.

How can a developer audit script tags?

An agency can extract addresses from the storefront, then query the Admin API for an app it maintains.

Check the storefront with curl

Run this command in a shell with curl, grep and sed available. Replace the example domain with the live store.

curl -s https://your-store.com/ | grep -o 'var urls = \[[^]]*\]' | grep -oE 'https?:[^"]+' | sed 's|\\/|/|g'

It extracts addresses from the var urls list and unescapes slashes. Some addresses retain \u0026 where the page has &; the domain stays readable.

Empty output means the command found no matching list. Check the page manually before concluding there are no tags. A password page or changed HTML format can also produce an empty result.

Query script tags through the Admin API

For an app your agency maintains, run this GraphQL Admin API query using that app's authenticated session:

query {
  scriptTags(first: 50) {
    nodes {
      id
      src
      displayScope
    }
    pageInfo {
      hasNextPage
      endCursor
    }
  }
}

src gives the address, displayScope identifies where the tag was intended to load and id identifies the record.

The query requests up to 50 records. If hasNextPage is true, fetch the next page using after with the returned endCursor.

The query returns only tags accessible to that app, not every app's tags on the store.

The official scriptTags reference documents its arguments and fields.

Once the replacement works, the app developer can use scriptTagDelete to remove the old record. This operation requires the appropriate script tag access.

What should you do with scripts nobody owns?

Unknown ownership needs investigation before removal.

An installed app is no longer used

Ask whether the business still needs its features. Check for connections to tracking, customers or store operations before uninstalling.

Uninstalling removes the app's script tags. Some apps leave theme code behind, so check the app listing or support instructions for additional cleanup.

Make code changes on a duplicate theme, not the live theme.

An old agency created a custom app

Some stores use admin-created custom apps for outside services or older integrations.

These apps cannot use Shopify app extensions or web pixels. Whoever maintains the integration must move its storefront script into the theme, using a custom Liquid block where possible or the code editor otherwise.

Editing theme code takes the theme off its automatic upgrade path. The service can instead supply a replacement app that supports extensions.

No installed app matches the domain

Contact likely vendors through Settings > Apps. Send the full script address and ask whether their app owns it.

Ask what replacement they provide and whether it needs activation.

Avoid deleting unfamiliar code until you know its purpose.

For help identifying owners and coordinating replacements, the Shopify script tag audit and cleanup service covers this work.

What should you check if Shopify script tags stop working?

If a widget disappears, check its app status, the published theme's App embeds panel and the storefront's asyncLoad list.

Before March 1, 2027, a failure can come from the app, theme settings or another integration issue.

After the deadline, check whether the app has supplied a replacement and whether the merchant activated it.

For analytics, verify events using the vendor's supported testing tools.

What is the migration checklist?

Use this checklist for each store you maintain.

  • [ ] Open the live storefront and find the asyncLoad script tag addresses.
  • [ ] Record each domain, full URL and suspected app in the inventory table.
  • [ ] Match every script to an installed app or confirm its owner with support.
  • [ ] Decide whether the feature is still required and which replacement it needs.
  • [ ] Ask the vendor or developer to prepare the replacement without disabling the working feature prematurely.
  • [ ] Activate required app embeds on the published theme and check any other theme scheduled for publication.
  • [ ] Verify each widget or tracking feature, then have the responsible app remove its old script tag where appropriate.
  • [ ] Check the storefront page source again after the changes to confirm the expected old addresses are gone.
  • [ ] Repeat the storefront and feature checks on or after March 1, 2027.

What should you check after removing the old scripts?

Check that required widgets work and analytics events are not duplicated.

Use the Core Web Vitals budget calculator to plan loading and interaction budgets if replacement scripts add JavaScript work.

Compare field data with lab measurements using the guide to why PageSpeed can look good while Core Web Vitals fail.

Keep the completed inventory with the store's maintenance records.

articles.title: Your GitHub review is still pending
articles.author: Nikita
articles.description:
A teammate kept leaving reviews half done. He'd open a pull request, add a few comments and move on without clicking "Submit review". The comments sat there marked "Pending". Only he could see them. The author waited for feedback that was already written.

It's an easy mistake. GitHub saves each comment the moment you add it, so it feels like you're done. People have been asking GitHub to make this clearer since 2022.

So I built Unsubmitted Review Alert. It notices the pending review and won't let you walk away from it quietly.

Reading the page

The extension asks for nothing beyond github.com: no token, no network requests, no storage. So the page is the only source of truth.

The best signal on it is the counter on GitHub's "Submit review" button, because GitHub's own React state renders it:

// content.js
const REVIEW_BUTTON = 'button[class*="ReviewMenuButton"]';
const REVIEW_BUTTON_COUNTER = '[data-component="ButtonCounter"]';

const count = toInt(reviewButton.querySelector(REVIEW_BUTTON_COUNTER));

Snippets in this post are trimmed for reading. The full source is on GitHub.

One rule from day one: never match the word "Pending" in the page. GitHub uses it elsewhere, and a reminder that fires for nothing gets uninstalled.

Four ways to leave

GitHub mostly doesn't load new pages. Clicking a tab swaps the content in place, so the browser's "Leave site?" dialog never fires. One "are you sure?" turned into four guards:

  1. Link clicks. A capture listener on window, before GitHub's router.
  2. Turbo visits. turbo:before-visit, which Turbo lets you cancel.
  3. Back and Forward. The Navigation API's navigate event.
  4. Close, reload, new URL. beforeunload, Chrome's own dialog.

Clicks are the easy one. React listens at the root of the app and Turbo on the document, so a capture listener on window runs before both:

// content.js
function onClickCapture(event) {
  // ...is it a plain click on a link that leaves this pull request?
  if (!confirmLeaving()) {
    event.preventDefault();
    event.stopImmediatePropagation();
  }
}

window.addEventListener('click', onClickCapture, true);

GitHub's keyboard shortcuts, like g i for Issues, click a link under the hood, so they land here too.

The Back button

This one was a real gap. If you got to the pull request from the PR list, Back stays inside GitHub's app. No page unload, no beforeunload, no prompt. popstate fires after the fact, so it's too late.

The Navigation API fires navigate before the history change reaches the page:

// content.js
navigation.addEventListener('navigate', (event) => {
  if (event.navigationType === 'traverse' && event.destination.sameDocument &&
      event.cancelable && leavesPendingPr(event.destination.url) && !confirmLeaving()) {
    event.preventDefault();
  }
});

Cancel it there and popstate never fires. GitHub's router never hears about the Back press, so the URL and the page stay in sync.

No trapping. Cancelling a Back step uses up the page's user activation (HTML spec). Press Back twice and you're out, which is why the code checks event.cancelable instead of assuming.

The bug that wasn't mine

Then I tested on a real review. Discard it from the Overview tab, and the bar stays until you reload.

The API said the review was gone. But GitHub's own button still said "2", and the comments still said "Pending". The extension wasn't wrong about the page. The page was wrong.

So I read the code GitHub ships for the review box. In my own words, Discard does this:

if not confirm("Are you sure you want to cancel? You will lose all your pending comments.")
  stop                         # the box stays open
mark the Discard button as loading
send DELETE for the pending review
on error:   show the error, keep the box open
on success: Files changed reloads the page
            Overview closes the box. Nothing else.

Submitting clears GitHub's local pending state. Discarding doesn't, and on Overview nothing reloads to hide it.

That gave me two signals I could trust. The Discard button goes into data-loading="true" only after you confirm. The box closes only on success.

// content.js
// Runs before GitHub's own click handler, which asks confirm() synchronously.
function watchDiscard(button) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (button.getAttribute('data-loading') !== 'true') return;
    discardState = { prKey, staleCount, done: false };
  }, 0);
}

The setTimeout(..., 0) is the trick. My listener runs before GitHub's, so nobody has answered the confirm yet. By the next task the button is either loading or it isn't. Once the box closes, the stale count is ignored until the page shows a different one.

Matching GitHub's theme

The bar lives in a shadow root, so GitHub's CSS can't break it. But custom properties inherit through the shadow boundary, and all: initial doesn't reset them. So the bar reads GitHub's own color variables:

/* content.js (the bar's stylesheet) */
:host { all: initial; }
.bar {
  background: var(--bgColor-default, #ffffff);
  color: var(--fgColor-default, #1f2328);
}

Testing without spamming GitHub

The content script only runs on github.com, so the fake pages have to live there. Playwright can route a real URL to a fixture:

// test/e2e.cjs
await context.route('https://github.com/**', (route) =>
  route.fulfill({ contentType: 'text/html', body: FIXTURES[new URL(route.request().url()).pathname] }));

The real extension loads into Chrome for Testing, sees the real origin, and touches no real pull request. A second suite runs against public pull requests with GitHub's real routers.

Try it

  • Chrome Web Store
  • Source on GitHub
  • A pull request to try it on

With Chrome's Enhanced protection on, the install dialog may say the extension "is not trusted by Enhanced Safe Browsing". Chrome says that about new publishers for the first few months (Google's explanation).

If it misses a case or nags when it shouldn't, open an issue.

articles.title: Scoring a daily game by rarity, not by a fixed answer key
articles.author: 尚毅段
articles.description:
Most daily games have one answer. You type it, the game says yes or no, and the streak continues. That model breaks as soon as the answer space is open-ended.

ZomZam gives one prompt a day and about two minutes to name as many things as you can. There are roughly 27 hidden answers per board, seven hints, and a new board at 00:00 UTC. The score is based on rarity: a common answer is worth less than one almost nobody else thought of. There is no fixed answer key to compare against.

The parts that are not obvious

Normalization comes first. If the prompt is "things you can ride", bike, Bike, bikes and a bike should not be four separate answers. Case folding, trimming, and simple plural handling get you most of the way; synonyms are a judgement call and usually belong in a small alias table rather than a general NLP pipeline.

Duplicates are a scoring problem, not a validation problem. Two players naming the same thing is the point. The scorer needs to know how often an answer appeared, not whether it is "correct".

Hints change the score. A hinted answer should not count the same as an unhinted one, or the seven hints become a free score multiplier.

The archive is a content decision. Keeping every past board for 90 days means the prompts and answer sets have to be stored, not regenerated. Regenerating from a seed sounds elegant until you change the normalization rules and old scores no longer reproduce.

What I would test before adding features

  • Two players typing the same answer with different casing or plural forms should score as a match.
  • A hinted answer and an unhinted answer should not produce the same score.
  • Replaying an archived board should reproduce the original score exactly.
  • A board should still be playable if the hint table fails to load.

The game is at zomzam.com if you want to see the current shape of it. The interesting engineering is not the prompt; it is making an open-ended answer space behave like a scored game without pretending there is one right answer.

articles.title: i built a gta 6 cheat site you can use from the ps5 browser with a controller
articles.author: Bro Explains
articles.description:
gta 6 came out this week and every cheat list i found was a 2 MB page full of ads that's painful to read on a phone, and basically unusable from the console's own browser. so i made vice6.codes, a list of every gta 6 cheat that's meant to be used with a controller in your hand.

some stuff i learned building it:

no framework, no bundler, no dependencies

the whole site is one json file (data/cheats.json) and a node script that turns it into plain html. no react, no build tool, npm install installs nothing. the home page is about 17 KB gzipped and there's no web font, no third-party script, no tracking cookies.

a code only gets marked "confirmed" when 3 independent guides list the same sequence, and the build fails if the data breaks a rule (like a "not found" cheat that somehow has a code).

controller navigation in console browsers

this was the hard part. the ps5 and xbox browsers do give you a cursor, but it's slow. what works better:

  • spatial navigation: the d-pad / arrow keys move focus to the nearest element in that direction, measured with getBoundingClientRect(), instead of tab order
  • gamepad api: square / x focuses search, triangle / y switches ps5 and xbox buttons, L1 / R1 cycle categories
  • big focus rings, and 44px targets everywhere

the browser's user agent says PlayStation or Xbox, so the page switches to controller mode before first paint.

real button glyphs without images

the d-pad, face buttons and bumpers are one inline svg sprite, generated at build time. each code renders as <use> references, so 60+ cards of button sequences cost almost nothing, and the ps5/xbox toggle just swaps which symbols the page shows.

small seo things that mattered

  • page dates come from the data, not the build time. if your sitemap says every page changed on every deploy, google learns to ignore it
  • meta descriptions get trimmed to whole sentences under 160 characters
  • llms.txt and a public cheats.json so ai assistants and bots can read the list without scraping
  • an RSS feed of new codes, for discord bots

if you play gta 6, the list is at vice6.codes. 19 of 61 codes are known so far. if you've built anything for console browsers i'd love to hear what you ran into.

articles.title: Web Weekly #202 (#blogPost)
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
Guten Tag! Guten Tag! 👋

Have you heard that ariaNotify is now baseline newly available? And do you wonder if JPEG XL is better than AVIF? And what's your take on Safari's new adaptive dark mode?

Turn on the Web Weekly tune and find some answers below. Enjoy!

::: song by="Pablo" title="Modeselektor - Sónar Festival 2026" youtube="tXzWwMk-0Ak" I love Modeselektor, an iteration of Apparat as Moderat, and this trippy one long hour concert at Sónar is energizing. :::

Do you want to share your favorite song with the Web Weekly community? Hit reply; there are two more songs left in the queue.

Deno and Astro joined Cloudflare. Nuxt and Svelte belong to Vercel. Tailwind and Remix joined Shopify. Anthropic acquired Bun, and OpenAI got the people from Pierre Computer Company (I'm just calling them out because they do very cool stuff).

And then there's Geoff. Geoff as in Geoff Graham, the editor of CSS-Tricks. After DigitalOcean bought the site that we all visited daily from Chris Coyier, it looked like another project was going to die because DigitalOcean seemed to have lost interest in it.

Not with Geoff, though, because he bought back CSS-Tricks from DigitalOcean. I have no idea about the deal size, but, oh boy, I definitely didn't see this one coming. And, of course, Geoff has big plans!

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone, no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

Many people shared that this feels like a long-awaited win for us, the bloggers, the educators. And I must admit I also felt a bit of encouragement after hearing the news. Maybe there's still a place for blogging, sharing, and learning together.

So, thank you, Geoff, for pushing forward. I really, really, really hope that this works out for you. And selfishly for us! ❤️

If you enjoy Web Weekly, share it with your friends and family.

  • 🦋 Bluesky
  • 🐘 Mastodon
  • 💼 LinkedIn

A quick "repost" really helps this indie newsletter out. Thank you! ❤️

Web Weekly Housekeeping

It's been quiet the last couple of weeks, so I want to apologize to my supporters for the silence. Thank you all for supporting Web Weekly on GitHub Sponsors and Patreon. ❤️

Something that made me smile this week

I don't know when or how I discovered Robert's blog. It feels very... wholesome? Browsing around gave me some good old blogging vibes. Robert also runs monthly themes, and this month's theme is "knowember".

If you're curious, here's my quick Knowember post.

Participate

No code

  • becoming yourself is a social project → "Most of us are surrounded by more care, intelligence, and help than we know how to access. Maybe part of reaching your potential is learning how to become easier to help."
  • Bug blindness → "I've seen people and teams with a high degree of quality blindness ship things that have reduced or even no chance of success because of product quality issues"
  • Writing to me with AI → "I really dislike this vibe on the internet right now. It feels like I’m constantly having to avoid being “tricked.”"

A nice abstraction

That's a nice quick tip. Lean described how to turn document.currentScript into an inline templating engine. Love it!

Replace it!

For the image nerds: JPEG XL vs AVIF

You might have heard that JPEG XL is now supported by all major browsers. Should you use it? Jake put out a massive article comparing the new format with AVIF. Be warned, the article is very long, but the tl;dr at the top has you covered.

Choose wisely

Should buttons have cursor: pointer?

So, do you use cursor: pointer for buttons? I'm strongly in favor of doing this, but as it turns out, some people have strong opinions on the matter.

Decide

Rebuilding flex-wrap: balance

flex-wrap: balance; is so far only shipping in Chromium. If you still want to achieve balanced flex layouts, Ahmad shared some ways to come up with similar results.

Be balanced

The wonderful weird web – The nicest place

If today's one of those days when you could use a hug, you'll find one at the nicest place on the internet. Love the old-school vibes of the site.

Get a hug

Upcoming: headingoffset

Granted, it's not prime time yet for headingoffset (shipping in Firefox 162 first) and :heading(), but adjusting heading levels is a feature we've needed since the failed outline algorithm. Let's see when the other browsers pick this up!

Control your headings

The Navigation API

The Navigation API has been available in all browsers since January. Do you use it?

If not, Ollie went on a tour to describe what you can do with it. The posts are quick reads and give you a good idea of what's possible. Thank you, Ollie!

  • The navigate event
  • Initiating navigations with the Navigation API
  • Focus Management with the Navigation API
  • Preventing same-document and cross-document navigation

.PropFLIP

If you've been in the game long enough, you might remember the FLIP technique. FLIP allows you to use CSS transitions for animations that you would usually need JavaScript for. Now, the technique is from 2015, so there must be a more modern version, right?

That's what Adam was after, and he describes a modern approach to FLIP using @property.

Flip it!

Move all these grid items

And speaking of moving things around, did you know that you can use and transition anchor-positioned grid items? That's some fancy stuff!

Move them

A fancy range slider

As usual, I've no idea how Temani does it, but what you see above is a CSS-only input of type range, an output element, and a label. I've got no words!

Pick a value

Safari's new adaptive dark mode

If you're a Safari user and are bothered by bright websites, Safari 27.3 beta introduced a new feature to automatically turn bright websites dark. The feature respects color-scheme so that it doesn't clash with your dark mode styles, and if you want to disable the feature entirely, <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> is your friend.

Go dark

And apparently, Chrome ships an auto dark mode feature behind chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark, too. I wonder how many bug reports come in when browsers change how sites look natively.

No AI Slop: A Manifesto

Nothing more to add here than some quotes from the manifesto.

Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.

When an agent wrote something we're sending, we make that clear, and we check the parts that matter before it goes out.

Human time and attention is incredibly valuable, so we optimize for using it wisely.

Don't be a slop cannon

Random MDN – :state()

From the unlimited MDN knowledge archive...

I gotta be honest here: I hadn't seen :state() before. Dave explained how he uses "pseudo-pseudo-classes" to build interactive component demos and well... today I learned :state() is a web component thing.

Give state

New on the baseline

It feels like browser vendors are still on fire, and it's hard to keep up with all the new features shipping. So here are some calm and easy-to-digest baseline updates. 🫣

  • Baseline newly available: ariaNotify
  • Baseline widely available: AbortSignal.any

Classifieds & friends

Web Weekly reader David is working on Pour. Pour is a WCAG 2.2 accessibility audit engine written from the W3C specifications. If you care about accessibility, which I'm sure you do, you should check it out!

Three valuable projects to have a look at

  • syabro/neat-annotations – Hand-drawn CSS annotations for inline content.
  • vercel-labs/portless – Replace port numbers with stable, named local URLs.
  • nilbuild/tinyhand – A tiny hand on a stick that points at things on your Mac screen. 😅

A new Tiny Helper

Back in the day, some people had the hobby of doing CSS art with the goal to draw things in a single div. The trick was to use multiple box-shadow or background values on the elements. I never tried creating these, but it can't be easy.

If you want to get into the game for some relaxation though, "Gradient Layers" helps you create and debug all these CSS declarations.

Be a CSS artist

Find more single-purpose online tools on tiny-helpers.dev.

Thought of the week

I 100% agree with Robin's take here.

The developers who thrive in this era will not be the ones with the highest output. They will be the ones whose output other people are glad to receive. Everyone else is generating work and calling it productivity.

Did you learn something from this issue?

❤️ If so, join 58 other Web Weekly supporters and give back with a small monthly donation on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

This is all, friends!

Loved this email? Hated this email? I want to hear about it!

If you think something needs improvement or something sparked some joy, reply to this email because I want to know more!

And with that, take care of yourself - mentally, physically, and emotionally.

I'll see you next week! 👋

articles.title: test v1.2.0
articles.author: github-actions[bot]
articles.description:
Minor Changes

  • t.useFakeTimers() now fakes Date, performance.now(), setImmediate()/clearImmediate(), and AbortSignal.timeout() along with the timer functions, so wall-clock code such as expiry checks and timestamps can be tested without injecting a clock. While fake timers are active, Date.now(), new Date(), and performance.now() read the fake clock and move forward only with advance() or advanceAsync(). new Date(value), Date.parse(), Date.UTC(), and instanceof Date keep working. Immediates fire on the next advance(), and AbortSignal.timeout(ms) signals abort with a TimeoutError once the fake clock reaches ms. (#12203)

    Like Node's mock timers, the fake Date starts at the Unix epoch (0) and performance.now() starts at 0. Tests that used fake timers while reading the real Date, or while relying on real immediates or AbortSignal.timeout(), now see fake time instead. Pass the new now option to start at a specific time:

    let timers = t.useFakeTimers({ now: new Date('2030-01-01T00:00:00Z') })

  • Added data-property mocking with mock.property() and t.mock.property(), including read/write records, one-access value overrides, and descriptor restoration. Added getter and setter spies through mock.getter(), mock.setter(), and the fourth mock.method() argument. Exported MockTracker as the shared type for standalone and test-context mocks. (#12225)

    Test-context accessor and property mocks restore in reverse installation order after cleanup callbacks, even when a test or cleanup callback fails. Method mocks layered over getter spies preserve the accessor's backing value. Method, accessor, and property mocks can be created while Array.isArray is mocked, with array argument checks preserved.

  • Added public TestFn and TestMeta types for reusable test callbacks and metadata, with linked API documentation for the test body and its options. (#12226)

  • Add new t.waitFor(condition, { interval, timeout }) API to retry assertions until they pass. Polling stops when the test ends. See Polling Assertions for usage. (#12224)

Patch Changes

  • Fix several gaps in t.useFakeTimers(): (#12203)

    • clearTimeout() and clearInterval() now cancel real timers created before fake timers were enabled. Previously the fakes ignored those timers, so a test with a timeout option that enabled fake timers left its real timeout timer running after it finished, which later aborted the test's signal and kept the process alive.
    • setTimeout() and setInterval() now pass extra arguments to the callback.
    • In Node, fake timers return handles with ref(), unref(), hasRef(), and refresh(), so code that calls .unref() on a timer no longer throws. Clearing an expired timeout's handle prevents refresh() from reactivating it.
    • Calling t.useFakeTimers() again restores the previous clock before starting a new one, so cleanup restores the original Date. Repeated restore() calls have no effect.
    • Restore fake timers synchronously on abort and before user cleanup callbacks. Finished or aborted contexts cannot enable another clock, and runner deadlines keep using real timers.
    • Reject overlapping clocks, roll back failed installations, and restore the original property descriptors without reinstalling fakes beneath spies. Restoration attempts every property, reports failures, and permits retrying failed properties.
    • Keep fake timer IDs unique across clocks so clearing a stale numeric handle cannot cancel a later test's timer.
    • Fake AbortSignal.timeout(ms) validates its argument synchronously using Node's numeric integer range of 0 through 4294967295 in every runtime.

  • Fix test and lifecycle hook timeouts stalling under fake timers and prevent late timeouts from aborting completed test signals. (#12224)

articles.title: The top 10 things AI gets wrong in web development
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
#​811 — November 17, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

npkill 1.0: Not Just for node_modules Anymore — npx npkill has long offered a way to find and remove waste from node_modules folders. Its first release in two years now also hunts down caches and build outputs like .next and .turbo, with 'profiles' for 20 ecosystems. If you're new to the tool, its homepage provides a good introduction.

Juan Torres

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous shows the exhaustive impact of every PR, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

UI SDK: Headless UI Behaviors for React, Vue, Svelte, & Solid — A new library from shadcn and Vercel that provides 50+ accessible, low-level behaviors, like roving focus, typeahead, popups, and drag and drop, that you compose into components (for several frameworks, plus Web Components).

Vercel

💡 𝕏 As shadcn says: "You and I don't need the same interfaces. We need the same interface behaviors." The idea is an agent, say, can generate whatever UI suits a task, with reusable focus, keyboard, and accessibility behaviors built in.

IN BRIEF:

  • Solid 2.0 is now stable, with 2.0.0 now on npm and the docs updated to match. There's no official announcement post (beyond the earlier Solid 2.0 RC posts) so expect more on this soon.

  • The Chrome team has proposed a Cross-Origin Storage API for sites to share large assets like AI models and WASM modules, so users would only have to download them once.

  • The cloud-based JavaScript hosting service Val Town is winding down with services ending January 10 and the code being open sourced in February.

  • The Bun team has published a dense technical tour of how its in-development ahead-of-time compiler works.

RELEASES:

  • Prettier 3.10 – The code formatter now supports the latest JavaScript proposals and new Flow syntax, and adds an opt-in plugin that swaps in the Zig-based Yuku's JS/TS parsers for speed.

  • 🎨 p5.js 2.4 – The creative coding library expands its SVG and 3D model support. Here's a starter sketch if you want to play quickly.

  • 🔒 Node.js v26.13.1 (LTS), v24.22.3 and v22.23.5 – The security releases we mentioned last week fix an HTTP/2 flaw that lets clients crash a server and an HTTPS bug that can leak other connections' memory.

  • PixiJS 3D – The popular 2D rendering library's official 3D engine is now in open beta. It's WebGPU-first, with a WebGL 2 fallback.

📖  Articles and Videos

📊 e18e's Ongoing Benchmarks of JavaScript Meta-Frameworks — The e18e performance initiative tracks releases of frameworks across the ecosystem (e.g. Nuxt, Astro, SvelteKit, SolidStart, and more), measuring everything from install size and build times to rendering speed. This dashboard is the place to dive in.

e18e

🤖 The Top 10 Things AI Gets Wrong in Web Development — The Chrome team examines where coding agents fall back on dated techniques, like hand-rolled focus traps instead of inert and JS overlays instead of popover, alongside gaps in passkey implementations and XSS defenses. A handy checklist for humans too.

Philip Walton (Google)

AI Security for Modern JavaScript & TypeScript — Traditional tools miss logic gaps. SonarQube Hunter Agent catches broken access control in your JS/TS CI/CD pipeline.

SonarSource sponsor

How a Third-Party Script Turned Malicious on Major Sites — An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely's A/B testing platform to inject a (now removed) malicious script into pages served to end users. Scott's analysis found it on sites including Zoom, the BBC, and GitLab, and shows how CSP can, and did, help.

Scott Helme (Report URI)

💡 Third-party scripts are an increasingly common attack vector, as Polymarket's users recently found. If you load any, brush up on CSP and Subresource Integrity, and if you provide them, see how Fathom secures theirs.

How Promises Really Resolve, Explained via a WebKit Bug — A contrived promise that should have thrown instead caused Bun and Safari (both of which use JavaScriptCore) to hang. Alistair fixed the bug and uses it to explain what resolve() actually does and why resolved isn't 'a real promise state'.

Alistair Smith

The Web Is More Than Enough — A reminder of how the vast array of powerful web platform APIs enables the development of complex apps in the browser, particularly as AI reduces the headaches involved in tying them together.

Paul Ford

Your JS Error Is Lying to You — Why can JSON.stringify(err) unexpectedly leave you with {}? Gabor presents a tour of what an Error holds, and how much of that makes it through stack traces, cause chains, worker boundaries, and loggers like Pino and Winston.

Gabor Koos

📄 How 13,000 Local Variables in a Function Overflowed V8's Stack – And why would that ever happen? It was the output of an OCaml to JS transpiler… :-) Jérôme Vouillon

📄 A Universal XSS in uBlock Origin via Its Element Picker – Leans on an interesting (and now fixed) postMessage and iframe exploit chain. Smitty van Bodegom

📄 Migrating 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in Three Weeks Daniele Rossino

🛠 Code & Tools

BrowserPod 4.0: A Linux-Like MicroVM for the Browser — A WASM-powered sandbox that runs Node, npm, git, and bash in the browser. Previously a metered service, v4.0 is free for any use, though it's not open source, and you must load it via their CDN (but no account or API key is needed).

Leaning Technologies

💡 Going somewhat deeper, Nitro creator Pooya Parsa has compiled the actual Linux kernel to WebAssembly (repo). It boots to a shell in under a second in modern browsers, or via npx unkernel (tip: use halt to exit!).

Debug Errors and Agents Faster: Sentry Changelog Live — A walkthrough of what’s new in debugging, from fixing prod bugs with Seer to tracing your agents. Register today.

Sentry sponsor

Kitesurf: Cloudflare's Browser Engine Now Open Source — An experimental browser for agents we featured in August. Mostly written in TypeScript and runs JavaScript in V8 isolates on Workers, with Rust compiled to WASM for layout and painting. There's no Chromium, and Puppeteer can drive it.

Cloudflare

File Viewer: A Multi-Format File Viewer for Internal Apps — Read-only views for Office, PDF/OFD, CAD, archives, email and other complex formats, with integrations for React, Vue, and Svelte. The docs site has demos showing off the formats covered.

Flyfish Dev

Flashwright: A Faster, API-Compatible Playwright Fork — Keeps Playwright's API and test runner, but reuses a browser context per worker and doesn't wait for animations to settle, plus similar tricks. Benchmarks show a ~2-4x speedup, while this post explains how it works.

Codebeast

React Flow 13: The Node-Based UI Library Gets Faster — The first major release in two years cuts re-renders in large flows, with new useNode and useEdge hooks. Vue Flow has joined the xyflow family too.

xyflow

  • SlickGrid 6.0 (above) – Long-standing data grid component. Now with zero dependencies, plus pinning on all four sides and sticky rows and columns. Examples and introductions on the project homepage.

  • XState v6 Beta – First beta of the state machine/actor library's next major version. The core API is considered stable and you can try it with xstate@beta.

  • 🕹️ Excalibur 1.0 – After 13 years, the 2D TypeScript game engine reaches v1 with 2D lighting, a plugin API, and a rebuilt Web Audio mixer. Sample games here.

  • 🕹️ JSNES 3.0 – JavaScript NES emulator. Now has a cycle-accurate core that passes all 134 'AccuracyCoin' tests. There are playable demos here.

  • type-fest 6.0 – Popular collection of essential TypeScript types (listed here). v6.0 adds 120 new types and requires TypeScript 6.

  • Fontkit 3.0 – Advanced font engine for Node and the browser. Now ESM-only, with a new core export so you can ship only the formats needed.

  • dts-bundle-generator 10.0 – A tool to tree-shake and bundle a project's TypeScript declarations into one file.

📰 Classifieds

📄 Parsing PDFs for a RAG or invoice pipeline? Foxit compares 10 document parsing APIs on output format, billing units and accuracy claims.

🌙 Agents can test mobile code at 3am. Expo Simulators gives them cloud simulators, so the loop runs while you sleep.

Stop being the middle manager for your coding agents. CodeAF runs the org, and only what no manager can settle reaches you. #1 on DeepSWE.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • You Don't Need jQuery, the long-standing guide to replacing jQuery methods with plain JavaScript, has had a big v3.0 update. Internet Explorer fallbacks are out in favor of modern one-liners like el.replaceChildren(), structuredClone(), and Promise.withResolvers().

  • Adam Argyle shares PropFLIP, a take on FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) animations where four @property custom properties do the inverting and a CSS transition does the playing.

  • AWS has released AWS Emulator, an official local emulator you can point your AWS SDK or CLI at, covering hundreds of its service interfaces. It's largely aimed at agents, and was built with them too.

  • 🎂 Happy birthday to Svelte! Svelte turned ten years old on Monday (Rich Harris made its first commit on November 16, 2016).

articles.title: How X (Twitter) is rebuilding its web app
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
#​810 — November 10, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

How X (Twitter) is Rebuilding Its Web App — X is replacing 3 servers with one app built on React, Vite and Fastify. Yagiz, famed for his performance work on Node, explains the streaming architecture behind it, along with some bottlenecks they had to fix, like how hundreds of tiny JavaScript files slowed startup.

Yagiz Nizipli (X Engineering Blog)

Why Standard Webhooks Hit 118m npm Downloads a Month — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini all sign webhooks with Standard Webhooks, the open spec Svix started. That's one finding in the State of Webhooks 2027, where we scored 489 API companies on retries and signatures. Immediate download, no email required.

Svix sponsor

Parcel 3 Alpha: The Bundler Rewritten in Rust — A ground-up Rust rewrite of the popular bundler that the team reports is up to 100x faster than Parcel 2 at cold builds of React Spectrum. It runs as a standalone binary without Node, with support for native plugins written in Rust, Go or Swift, while JavaScript plugins run on an embedded QuickJS runtime.

The Parcel Team

IN BRIEF:

  • 📊 The State of JavaScript 2026 survey is now open. Share the features, libraries and tools you use and like, and discover a few new ones along the way. We'll share the results once they're out.

  • TypeScript 7's Go-powered compiler now has an experimental WebAssembly build which already powers an early TypeScript Playground v2.

  • ESLint now officially lints shell scripts with the @eslint/shell plugin adding ShellCheck-like rules for Bash, sh and mksh.

RELEASES:

  • Playwright 1.65 – The browser testing tool's test runner can now run under Bun, plus there's a new failures reporter.

  • Storybook 11 Beta – The UI component workshop gets more agent-ready, with official skills, Claude/Codex plugins, headless CLI tools, and more.

  • 🔒 Vite has disclosed a critical remote code execution flaw affecting dev servers exposed to the network via --host or server.host. Upgrade to 8.3.7, 8.2.5, 8.1.7, 7.3.8 or 6.4.6.

  • 🔒 Next.js 16.4.5 and 15.5.29 fix seven security issues, including a high-severity cross-tenant cache disclosure.

  • 🔒 Node.js security releases are due tomorrow (or shortly after) for the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines.

📖  Articles and Videos

Experiments with Multithreaded JavaScript — What would JavaScript look like if threads could share objects directly? Former TC39 delegate Erik Arvidsson explores three approaches: in a Porffor fork, as a TypeScript library with an ownership checker, and as an implementation of the TC39 structs proposal. Each has a playground to try.

Erik Arvidsson

The New JavaScript Features Between V8 14.6 and 15.6 — Node 27, released in alpha recently, is built on V8 15.6, and Joyee tours what that brings to developers, including Math.sumPrecise, new iterator methods, and some behavior changes in sorting, dates and promises, all with sample code.

Joyee Cheung

How to Build Your Own Automated Debugging Workflow — Connect your coding agent to Sentry and turn errors into fix PRs. See the guides and recipes in the resource hub.

Sentry sponsor

Spreading Liquid with three.js — A technical explanation of a 'liquid-spreading' effect originally built for a cosmetics site. The in-page demo is fun to play with and this could be handy if you want to create paint-like effects.

Misaki Nakano

Reviving Facebook's Abandoned JavaScript Optimizer — Prettier creator James Long put agents to work resurrecting Prepack, Facebook's attempt to make JavaScript faster by running it ahead of time. There's an experimental demo that shows off the gains on a sample React app.

James Long

Yavashark: Building a JavaScript Engine for 950 Days Straight — A solo developer's progress report on a Rust-based engine they're building that passes around 82% of test262 and can server-render a React app. There's a playground to try it for yourself.

Sharktheone

📄 A Fifth Object Shape Made the Same Loop Twice as Slow – V8's hidden classes and inline caches in action. Mohsen Fallahnejad

📺 ReactiveScript: Early Findings – A lengthy stream by Solid's creator on ReactiveScript, his experimental reactive UI language he first shared in 2021. Ryan Carniato

🛠 Code & Tools

EmbedPDF 3.0: A PDF Viewer for Any JavaScript App — An open-source PDF viewer for vanilla JavaScript, React, Vue, Svelte and Angular. The v3 rebuild offers a ready-made viewer, headless components for custom UIs, and a standalone PDF engine. Try the demo.

EmbedPDF

Embed an Office Editor Your App's AI Agent Can Use — DOCX/XLSX/PPTX editing in your app with your model and workflow. Agents make targeted edits, and users refine the file.

Thinkfree sponsor

chrome-capture: Record a Chrome Tab at 60-120fps to an MP4 File — It's been three years since we've linked to Paul Irish (once a frequent fixture in JavaScript Weekly!) but he's back with a neat, compact tool you can run with npx to record a Chrome tab at high quality including audio to an MP4 video.

Paul Irish

#​809 — November 3, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

The AI Cost of JavaScript Frameworks

Nolan Lawson had Claude build the same app five times in each of twelve JS stacks to test common "X is better for agents" claims. Costs varied significantly between runs, and Gautam Parab found that the observed cost ranges overlapped or touched for most pairs of frameworks.

But a clearer difference was in the median amount of JavaScript sent to browsers: 0KB for Astro, 18K for Hono+htmx, 36K for SvelteKit, and 115–142K for React Router, TanStack Start and Next.js. If you've gone "hands-free", Nolan asks, why stick to a particular stack you chose when you wrote all the code? His benchmark is on GitHub to try for yourself.

Nolan Lawson

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

Why Is This Fingerprinting Script 'Creating Bioweapons'? — A crawl of sites to collect canvas fingerprinting examples (which you can see, visually, at fingerprint.garden) found an anti-analysis technique where JavaScript identifiers were named after… taboo topics, with a prompt hidden in invisible Unicode, all designed to make LLMs refuse to work on the code!

Veritas

💡 Canvas fingerprinting is a technique that uses quirks of how different clients render canvas elements, in order to distinguish browser environments.

IN BRIEF:

  • 😄 Bartosz shares a creative way to generate strings and run code without parentheses or quotes. Good old JavaScript fun!

  • 📊 GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report has TypeScript as the most used language on GitHub by contributors (with JS at third), and ~44% of merged TypeScript PRs showing AI involvement. Plus a lot more besides.

Manu Nair (Microsoft)

Workshop: How to Implement Session Replay — Filters, custom tags, and sampling settings for finding the sessions that matter. Nov 5, 10am PT.

Sentry sponsor

Bruno Jurković

Timing Ten Design Systems, Then Fixing the Slow Ones — Den timed ten design systems (MUI, Ant Design, and Ionic among them) opening a 249-option select and ticking 100 checkboxes, then profiled the slow ones to find out why.

Den Odell

Using Bun? Dependabot Can't See Most of Your Dependencies — GitHub's dependency graph doesn't parse bun.lock, so Dependabot alerts cover only direct dependencies. Nicolas has some tips for improving matters.

Nicolas Charpentier (Shortcut)

📄 How Hard Is It to Check for Whitespace? – Why Java, Python and JavaScript disagree on what counts as whitespace. Sergey Tselovalnikov

📄 A Proposal: How to Hire Junior Engineers in the Age of AI – The npm co-founder thinks traditional coding interviews are dead. Laurie Voss

📄 How to Make postMessage Type-Safe in Under 350 Bytes Pavel Grinchenko (Evil Martians)

📄 The Web Can't Afford a JavaScript Runtime Monoculture Kate Holterhoff (RedMonk)

🛠 Code & Tools

Handwired: Compile Regular JavaScript into a Neural Net — A new mind-bender from Pretext's creator: a compiler that turns JavaScript into an exact network of ReLUs and matrix multiplies that run on the GPU. Demos include a 130-layer 'mini desktop' and a WebGPU search over 100K JSON documents.

Cheng Lou

SerpApi sponsor

Anthony Fu

djs: A New 'Suspend Anywhere' JavaScript Engine — Armin (of Flask fame) built an engine to run scripts in WebAssembly that can snapshot the VM's state and resume elsewhere, even mid-await.

Armin Ronacher

articles.title: Blake Watson on the state of the industry (#note)
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
Here's Blake sharing his feelings about AI, software development and where we're all heading. He wrote the article that's been on my TODO list for a while. Let me comment on some highlights.

I feel like I will be able to build things I never have been able to before, but at the same time, I have heightened fears about being replaceable or less valuable in my job. If all I’m doing is prompting an AI bot, why am I being paid so much?

100% this. I'm scared and worried that the skills I put so much time into building are worth nothing. I used to be proud of my deep platform knowledge. Turns out Claude knows more.

And on a bigger scale, "personal software" is really happening. My friends are building browser extensions and websites for their fantasy football leagues. They don't care about quality as long as it gets the job done. Occasionally they ask me things about the DOOM (DOM), which is funny and scary at the same time.

At what point does software still need someone who actually knows what they're doing? I guess we'll find out soon enough.

If you haven’t used one of these coding tools in the last six months, you probably don’t have a good idea of what they are capable of.

I admire people who are still holding out against this technology, I really do. If that's you, you rock! Unfortunately, I couldn't agree more with the statement above.

If your arguments about LLM quality and all the generated fake news (hallucinations) are based on Copilot tryouts around last Christmas, you'd better check again. Things have changed a lot.

I just have this icky feeling when I use it.

Same. I hate that I can create things without effort or understanding. I hate that there are days when I talk to agents all day. I hate that it seems like nothing matters anymore. I hate that everyone is pushing and pushing and pushing and nothing gets done.

I’m worried about being replaced, but maybe I’ll be even more valuable. [...] So I just go back and forth. I worry about it, but then I think everything will work out.

Yes. There are good weeks and then there are bad weeks.

Sometimes, I'm okay with "focusing on the outcome". Sometimes, I'm fine with the loss of the job that was my favorite thing to do. Sometimes, I have enough energy to change habits and find satisfaction and joy elsewhere.

But sometimes, man... sometimes the new world drives me nuts.

So, let's hope Blake is right and things will work out (somehow).

Reply to Stefan

Do you know what happens when you import the same module multiple times? Do you think we need a new poster element? And have you ever used the vary header to improve caching?

Turn on the Web Weekly tune and find some answers below. Enjoy!

::: song by="Dom" title="Twenty One Pilots - Center Mass" youtube="PAbv0MXFYgE" I really like the shift from a hip-hop style to a full rock ending, and the lyrics are well written around the topic of vulnerability and loss. :::

Do you want to share your favorite song with the Web Weekly community? Hit reply; there are three more songs left in the queue.

I try to avoid bringing up my mood about "all the vibes" too much in this newsletter, but the change in the industry is the stickiest topic ever. And regardless of whether the industry collapses or not, I don't think the technology will disappear. Cheap open source models can do certain things better and faster than I can. They'll probably survive, like it or not.

So here are my two AI takes for today.

AI makes projects with weak engineering culture fail much faster.

Florian describes the scenario of teams that are just shipping. They move fast but lose control quickly. I see that around me and it shows the real challenge if you're using AI for coding. It's just too easy to cover a lot of ground. Taking on the responsibility of understanding what's going on while establishing good practices and judgment will be one of the most important skills going forward. My brain wants all the shortcuts, and yours probably does too. Not taking them is the real challenge.

You need to find some way to leverage your expertise to do what the models can’t.

I was hesitant for a long time, but frankly I became too scared to ignore what's going on because it's still a long time until I'm ready for retirement.

That's why I follow what's happening closely and try things myself to know what's hype and what's real. It's obvious that the machines are pretty good at certain tasks. Busy work is one of them. But there are still areas they're "not great" at.

It's important to understand the technology's weak spots. I watch out for areas to apply my strengths. As Sean puts it, there will be areas in which you'll be better than the machines.

This topic is heated and emotional, so I just wanted to share where I'm at right now. I also guess there are many Web Weekly readers that aren't thrilled about the new world. If that's you, hang in there! And if you want to share your thoughts with me, you can always hit reply.

If you enjoy Web Weekly, share it with your friends and family.

  • 🦋 Bluesky
  • 🐘 Mastodon
  • 💼 LinkedIn

A quick "repost" really helps this indie newsletter out. Thank you! ❤️

Web Weekly Housekeeping

Last week, I shared the new Connection-Allowlist header and Nicolas told me that the implementation has already started in Firefox. 🎉

And because I mentioned complicated CSP configuration, Mark shared with me how the strict-dynamic directive can help tame all this CSP madness.

And of course, as always, I want to give a huge shoutout to the 58 Web Weekly supporters!

Thank you so much for supporting Web Weekly. Your small gestures really keep me going in the time of the slopocalypse. If you also want to support indie publishing, you can do so on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

Something that made me smile this week

Nothing spectacular: it's just Frank who drew his own emoji collection one by one. You can get it on frankmoji.com.

Express yourself

No code

  • Don't be nice → "If you hear enough people say something it somehow becomes 'just another opinion.'"
  • how to find meaning in ordinary days → "not all loneliness needs to be cured. some of it just needs to be sat with."
  • You should never be angry at work → "Angry engineers are rarely the ones holding the company together, but they’re also rarely useless."

The example.com redesign

So, example.com got a redesign. 👆 People asked why and the VP of IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) replied that it was to save bandwidth. The new site now enriches the page with a single s.js file so that bots, curls, or whatever can save some bytes. Wild!

Load less

Responsive iframes

Who would have thought that I'd plug an iframe change that I'm actually excited about? I had to deal with resizing iframes quite a bit, so this platform addition is more than welcome. So if you're updating iframe sizes manually, you'll dig this!

Be aware that responsive iframes are cutting-edge and Chromium-only so far.

Automatically resize

AI policies

You might have heard that Sindre, who maintains a gazillion open source projects in the JS ecosystem, closed external contributions. This means you can't simply contribute to his projects anymore.

Of course, I'm not maintaining that many or that successful projects, but I see myself making more and more things private on GitHub. I just can't be bothered anymore.

On top of that, I also receive five emails per week from "fake Web Weekly readers" who want to plug their posts and projects. The bold ones even include a personal agent signature. The new world is just wasting everyone's time.

Regardless, before closing everything, maybe adding an AI policy is worth a shot.

Define some rules

Kinda related side note: do you know that GitHub now highlights your projects' accessibility statements? 👏

Do we need a <poster> element?

Scott thinks so and is yet again on the journey of extending the web. Scott was also part of bringing lazy loading to videos, and he's on to the next topic: responsive images in video elements.

I love these stories.

Control the preview

The wonderful weird web – The restroom archive

The Restroom Archive is an ongoing repository of publicly accessible restrooms. [...] Currently, 40 archivists have documented 193 restrooms in 85 cities across 13 countries.

What? I have no words. 😅 And before you wonder, the site lists 3D models of restrooms. I checked seven restrooms and they were reasonably clean.

Take a break

The tricky vary header

Cloudflare added support for the vary header. It's fair if you now think "Alright, why would I care?". The post does a good job explaining what vary does and why caching is hard (obviously).

Control the cache

Import, import, and import

What happens when you call import('foo.js') twice? Joan explains how the module map works and that there will be only one network call. But what if the first import fails and you want to try again? That used to be tricky, but turns out, there's a spec change rolling out as we speak.

Overfetch

Modern Web Types

If you're using cutting-edge web features, you probably run into the situation that TypeScript doesn't know about new properties yet because it only includes types for features supported by two engines (TIL!). Philip was so annoyed by this that he released modern-web-types which includes features that are only supported by one engine.

But, as mentioned in the post, you shouldn't rely on TypeScript for feature detection or support info. That's where proper Baseline tooling comes in.

Ride the cutting edge

Some interop "things"

I think the submission of Interop focus areas for next year is closed by now, but you can still chime in and add your thumb to your favorites on GitHub.

The fine folks at Firefox also built a nice UI to rank your most preferred new web features. The data goes to the Firefox team as far as I understand.

And the web dev community is still around (❤️) and blogged about their favorite features, too.

  • My Interop 2027 picks from Paweł
  • My Interop 2027 Rankings from Declan
  • My top picks for Interop 2027 from Sara

And if you want to dive into this rabbit hole, the community links back and forth between all these posts. Love ya!

Random MDN – ::details-content

From the unlimited MDN knowledge archive...

Just a quick reminder: ::details-content is a thing these days.

Style the content

New on the baseline

The alpha() CSS function became Baseline newly available and Object.groupBy() is now widely available.

Three valuable projects to have a look at

  • zachleat/table-of-contents – A table of contents web component.
  • Homebrew/BrewUI – Homebrew's official macOS GUI.
  • Wox-launcher/Wox – A cross-platform launcher.

A new Tiny Helper

If you're looking for a quick way to create mockups with phones on a nice background, Sliick indeed looks slicker than many other tools that do that.

Do a photo shoot

Find more single-purpose online tools on tiny-helpers.dev.

Thought of the week

Here's Sean on playing company politics...

If you have powerful enemies at a company (for instance, the CTO or an influential VP doesn’t like you), quit.

Did you learn something from this issue?

❤️ If so, join 58 other Web Weekly supporters and give back with a small monthly donation on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

This is all, friends!

Loved this email? Hated this email? I want to hear about it!

If you think something needs improvement or something sparked some joy, reply to this email because I want to know more!

And with that, take care of yourself - mentally, physically, and emotionally.

I'll see you next week! 👋

Reply to Stefan
